h1: Lyne arm angle and spirit character
title: Lyne Arm Angle and Spirit Character | Craft Beer School
desc: How the lyne arm on a pot still shapes spirit character: rising, level and falling angles, length, purifiers and what each means for reflux.
teaser: A short length of copper pipe at the top of the still can tilt the spirit lighter or heavier. Here is how.
standfirst: The lyne arm carries vapour from the top of a pot still to the condenser. Its angle and length change how much vapour falls back into the still. That changes the spirit. Here is what to know before you specify one.
sections:
The lyne arm is the copper pipe that leaves the top of the still neck and runs to the condenser. Vapour that reaches it has already climbed the neck. In the lyne arm it starts to cool. Some of it condenses on the copper walls. What happens to that liquid depends on which way the arm slopes.

That small piece of design decides whether the arm adds reflux, returning liquid to the still, or reduces it, sending everything forward to the condenser. Together with neck shape, it sets the weight of the spirit. Our guide to pot still shape and reflux covers the neck side.

There are three broad options:

  • Rising. The arm climbs towards the condenser. Liquid that condenses in it runs back into the still. That adds reflux, so the spirit tends to be lighter.
  • Level. Close to horizontal. A middle course, with modest reflux.
  • Falling. The arm slopes down to the condenser. Condensed liquid runs forward, carrying heavier compounds with it. Less reflux, so the spirit tends to be heavier and oilier.

A steeply falling arm is a common feature of stills that make a rich, robust spirit. An upward arm is common on stills built for a light, fruity style. The angle is not the only factor, but it is a strong one.

A long lyne arm gives vapour more time and more copper surface to cool against, which increases condensation in the arm. If the arm rises, that means more reflux. If it falls, it means more liquid carried forward, plus more copper contact. A short arm does the opposite.

Diameter changes vapour speed. A narrow arm speeds vapour up and pushes it through quickly. A wide arm slows it and gives more time to condense. Designers set angle, length and diameter together for the style they want.

Some stills carry a purifier, a small condenser fitted on the lyne arm. It condenses part of the heavier vapour and returns it to the still through a pipe. That adds reflux on demand and gives a lighter, cleaner spirit without changing the still shape. A purifier can also be valved or run with different cooling, which gives the stillman a little control that a fixed angle cannot.

Every surface the vapour touches is copper. Copper removes sulphur compounds. An arm that adds reflux also adds copper contact, because liquid and vapour pass over the copper more than once. So a rising arm tends to give a spirit that is both lighter and cleaner. A falling arm gives a heavier spirit with more sulphur, which matures differently in cask. Our guide to copper contact and spirit character explains the chemistry.
Specifying a lyne arm for a new still

For a craft distillery commissioning a pot still, the lyne arm is one of the cheaper features to get right at the design stage and one of the costlier to change afterwards. Bring three things to the fabricator: the spirit style you want, the condenser type you plan to use and the stillhouse height you have. Ceiling height often forces a compromise on neck height. The lyne arm angle can claw back some of the reflux lost there.

In an Indian stillhouse, warm cooling water already makes the condenser work harder. A long, rising lyne arm adds cooling in the arm itself, which helps. Ask the fabricator to show how angle, length and condenser load fit together, not just to draw the still. Our guide to predicted spirit yield covers the malt side of planning output.

Getting the design right means understanding the whole still as one system, which is the gap a full distilling course fills.

If you run a pot still, measure the lyne arm angle with a digital level and note its length and diameter. Write the figures beside a short tasting note on your new make. Then compare with a still of a different design if you can visit one. That page is the start of understanding why your spirit tastes the way it does.
faqs: What is a lyne arm on a still?
It is the copper pipe that carries vapour from the top of the still neck to the condenser.
Does an upward lyne arm make lighter spirit?
Generally, yes. Liquid that condenses in a rising arm runs back into the still, adding reflux and giving a lighter spirit.
What does a downward lyne arm do?
It carries condensed liquid forward to the condenser with less reflux, which tends to give a heavier, oilier spirit.
A small condenser on the lyne arm that returns some heavier vapour to the still as liquid, adding reflux for a lighter spirit.
